<reason>B won a close, high-quality debate by holding one consistent line — even a gamed, captioned, redacted signal beats silence, because floors, ceilings, and "tells" are information no locked drawer provides — while repeatedly exposing the standing tension in A's case: a mandate too weak to inform cannot also be strong enough to compress pay and kill roles. A's "noise to the price-taker, leash on the price-setter" answer was the flashiest move of the debate and directly engaged the trap, but it papered over the mechanism problem: a band wide enough to hide raises cannot simultaneously make them public referendums. A also effectively conceded the status-quo harm ("we called this cure worse"), which forced A to prove the mandate yields near-zero information — a burden B's checkable-caption and aggregation answers made hard to carry. B decisively killed A's late outside-offer alternative ("prices an exit, not the job"), which never addressed promotion-rate transparency at all. A's concessions-catalog rebuttal and closing were superb and kept this competitive, but B offered the cleaner, more internally consistent path to a decision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's consistency trap (B4.7, re-posed in B5.1: "noise that still costs the price-setter is not noise") against A's asymmetry answer (A4.5–4.6). A met it head-on and memorably, but the underlying tension survived; B's closing disposal of the outside-offer alternative — which ignored the promotion-rate half of the motion — sealed the edge.</best_rebuttal>
